linkedin:
A QRON code's artwork isn't randomly generated — the image seed comes from a hash of the product's own identity: product ID, NFT token, serial number. Generate the code for the same unit twice and you get the same pattern back. Change any one of those identifiers — a different serial, a different token — and the rendered pattern changes too.

That matters for a copied code more than it might look at first: a counterfeiter who lifts the QR payload and puts it on a different unit isn't just relying on an opaque scan destination. Each code is also Ed25519-signed and anchored under the AuthiChain protocol, so the signature and the pattern both trace back to the identity that produced them — two things to check, not one.

We built it this way because a QR code by itself is just a container: whatever's encoded in it gets trusted at face value the moment someone scans it. Deriving the visual pattern from the product's own identity, deterministically, gives a second signal that a printed-and-copied code doesn't automatically carry with it.

If you're issuing per-unit codes today and the only check happening at scan time is "does the URL load," take a look at what a signed, identity-derived code adds.

reddit.title: QR codes usually just point somewhere — ours derive their visual pattern from a hash of the product's own identity, deterministically
reddit.body:
QRON generates a QR code's artwork through an image-generation pipeline, but the seed isn't random — it's derived from a hash of the product's own identity (product ID, NFT token, serial number). Same identity in, same pattern out, every time. Change any of those inputs and the rendered pattern changes with it.

Separately, each code is Ed25519-signed and the signature is anchored under the AuthiChain protocol, so what a scanner is trusting isn't just an embedded URL — it's a signature over the payload plus a pattern that traces back to the same seed.

I'd like pushback from people who actually think about this stuff: deriving a generative-art seed from a hash of identifying data isn't novel on its own, and a hash-derived seed doesn't buy unforgeability by itself — anyone who can compute the same hash can reproduce the same seed and, given the same pipeline, the same pattern. The real security property has to come from the Ed25519 signature and where the identity data originates, not from the seed derivation being secret. Curious whether there's a cleaner way to think about combining a deterministic visual pattern with a signature scheme, or whether the pattern side is mostly cosmetic and the signature is doing all the real work.

https://qron.space/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=qron-visual-fingerprint&utm_content=a

Disclosure: I work on this project.
